items.explain: dbt's Semantic Layer exposes metrics via a query API (GraphQL/SQL); tools query the layer, not raw tables, so definitions stay consistent.
items.q: dbt's Semantic Layer approach is:

choices: Define metrics once in the layer; certified vs uncertified metrics visible to consumers
items.explain: Governance = one definition + clear certification. Self-service still works, but consumers see which metrics are certified.
items.q: Semantic-layer governance in practice means:

choices: A slow-changing but shared definition that changes behind the API without breaking consumers
It must be a stored procedure
items.explain: Versioned metric definitions behind a stable API: the logic evolves, consumer queries don't break — like a well-designed API.
items.q: Changing a metric's definition safely under a semantic layer works because it is:

choices: Dimensions are descriptive attributes; measures are the numeric facts you aggregate — conflating them breaks drill-downs
items.explain: Dimension (region, product) vs measure (revenue, count): the semantic layer models both explicitly so aggregations and drill paths are correct.
items.q: In semantic modeling, the dimension/measure distinction matters because:

handsOnLab.brief: Design a semantic layer for the sample sales data: define 5 governed metrics, expose them to two different consumers, and prove the numbers match.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Learner can explain why the two consumers can't disagree once the layer is the only path to the metric.
handsOnLab.deliverable: The metric definitions (YAML/code), two consumer queries, and the matching-results proof.
steps: 1. List the 5 metrics stakeholders actually argue about (revenue, active customers, churn rate, average order value, gross margin). Write the exact definition of each in plain English first.
2. Implement them in one place: dbt metrics YAML, a Cube.js/Cube schema, or a well-tested SQL view layer — one definition per metric, versioned.
3. Build two consumers: (a) a dashboard query and (b) an ad-hoc analyst query, both going through the layer (no direct table access for these metrics).
4. Run both and compare results — they must match to the row. Then change one definition (e.g. revenue excludes refunds) and show both consumers update together.
5. Document the governance rules: who can certify a metric, how uncertified/experimental metrics are labeled, the deprecation process.
handsOnLab.title: Semantic layer design lab

choices: Introduce a semantic layer as the single governed metric path, migrate both tools to it, and certify the shared definitions — the dashboard gets faster AND the numbers agree
Tell one team to stop using their tool
Rebuild both dashboards from scratch in a third tool
mockTask.explain: The dispute is structural (two definitions), not political. A semantic layer fixes the root cause — one definition, all consumers — instead of arbitrating each fight.
mockTask.q: Marketing's dashboard says Q3 revenue is $4.2M; Finance's says $3.9M. Both are 'correct' under different definitions (gross vs net of refunds). The executive team asks you to end the argument permanently. Your move:

choices: //order/customer/name selects all customer/name descendants of any order node, at any depth
It selects the root element only
items.explain: // = descendant-or-self at any depth. This is the workhorse selector for finding nodes when you don't know (or care about) the exact path.
items.q: In XPath, //order/customer/name means:

choices: @ selects attributes; //book[@inStock='true'] filters book elements by their inStock attribute
items.explain: @ is the attribute axis. Predicate [@attr='value'] filters nodes — essential for XML feeds where status lives in attributes.
items.q: What does the @ do in //book[@inStock='true']?

choices: Declare the namespace and use the prefix in your XPath — default namespaces are NOT matched by unprefixed names
items.explain: The #1 XML gotcha: a default namespace means <order> is actually {ns}order. Register the namespace and query ns:order.
items.q: Your XPath returns nothing on a document that clearly has <order> elements. The document declares xmlns='http://example.com'. The fix:

choices: An XSLT stylesheet transforms XML to another format (XML, HTML, text) via template matching
items.explain: XSLT = XML transformation language. Templates match nodes and emit new structure — the standard way to reshape legacy XML feeds.
items.q: XSLT's role in a data pipeline is:

choices: text() selects the text node; normalize-space() trims whitespace — essential because pretty-printed XML is full of whitespace text nodes
Use string() on the root always
items.explain: Pretty-printed XML wraps every element in whitespace text nodes. normalize-space(text()) gives you the actual value.
items.q: Why do XML extraction queries so often use normalize-space(text())?

choices: Parse with an XML library (ElementTree/lxml), validate against the XSD if provided, extract with XPath — never regex
items.explain: Regex on XML breaks on nesting, namespaces, CDATA, and entities. A real parser + XPath handles all of it; XSD validation catches malformed feeds early.
items.q: A vendor sends a 50 MB XML feed nightly. The senior ingestion approach:

handsOnLab.brief: Ingest a real XML feed: validate it, extract it to a clean table with XPath, and transform a variant format with XSLT.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Learner can explain why the namespace declaration broke their first XPath and how they fixed it.
handsOnLab.deliverable: The parser script, the extracted table (CSV/Parquet), and the XSLT stylesheet.
steps: 1. Get a real XML sample: an RSS/Atom feed, a sitemap.xml, or a SOAP-style sample. Inspect it raw — note namespaces, attributes vs elements, nesting depth.
2. Validate: if an XSD/DTD exists, validate with lxml; log every validation error. If none exists, document the implied schema.
3. Extract with XPath: write selectors for the 6-10 fields you need (use //, predicates, @ for attributes, normalize-space). Load into a pandas/Polars frame.
4. Handle the namespace gotcha deliberately: write the query first without the namespace (watch it fail), then fix it with a registered prefix.
5. Write an XSLT stylesheet that transforms the feed's structure into your target schema (rename elements, flatten one nesting level). Apply it and diff the output.
handsOnLab.title: XML feed ingestion lab

choices: Negotiate the deprecation timeline, but immediately build a validated XPath/XSLT ingestion path for the XML — regex or string hacks on a 200 MB nested feed will silently corrupt data
Write a regex to pull the fields
Ask the vendor to also send JSON (and stall until they do)
Parse it with string split on '><'
mockTask.explain: Vendor timelines are aspirational; the data is real today. A proper XML parser handles namespaces, nesting, and entities correctly at 200 MB — regex does not.
mockTask.q: A critical vendor feed switches from JSON to a 200 MB nested XML format with namespaces next month ('JSON coming in Q2, maybe'). Your ingestion plan:

choices: The one chart type that answers the question with the least cognitive load — usually simpler than you think
items.explain: Chart selection is question-driven: trend → line, composition → bar/stacked, distribution → histogram. One clear chart beats a dashboard on a slide.
items.q: The right chart for an executive slide is:

choices: A takeaway title that states the conclusion ('Churn fell 18% after the fix'), not a description ('Churn chart')
items.explain: Executives read titles first. A conclusion-title lets them get the point without decoding the chart; the chart is the evidence.
items.q: An executive slide title should be:

choices: Directly on the chart: annotate the spike, label the key values, kill the legend where possible
items.explain: Annotation-on-chart removes the eye's round trip between legend and data. Label values directly, circle the insight, delete chartjunk.
items.q: Where do the key numbers go on a data slide?

choices: One idea per slide; 3-5 slides for the story (situation, insight, evidence, recommendation)
items.explain: The Pyramid/Minto structure: answer first, then supporting insights, each on its own slide. Backup goes in the appendix.
items.q: A 5-minute executive readout on your analysis should be structured as:

choices: High contrast, large fonts, meaningful alt text, no color-only encoding
items.explain: Accessibility is professionalism: colorblind-safe palettes, direct labels instead of legend-color-matching, fonts readable from the back row.
items.q: Accessible data slides require:

choices: python-pptx for programmatic, repeatable decks — templates, branded styles, data-driven charts from your analysis code
items.explain: python-pptx lets your analysis script generate the deck: same data, same branding, every refresh. Screenshots don't scale and break accessibility.
items.q: The monthly KPI deck takes 2 days of manual copy-paste. The senior fix:

handsOnLab.brief: Turn a real analysis into a 5-slide executive deck: takeaway titles, annotated charts, appendix backup — then present it in 5 minutes.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Learner can deliver the whole story from the slide titles alone (the squint test).
handsOnLab.deliverable: The .pptx file plus a 1-page speaker script.
steps: 1. Take a completed analysis (your M41 DuckDB lab or any prior module). Write the one-sentence answer a CEO needs. That's your title slide's takeaway.
2. Outline 5 slides: situation → key insight → evidence (the one chart) → what drove it → recommendation. One idea per slide.
3. Build each chart to answer its slide's question: right chart type, direct labels, annotated insight, no 3D, no legend-lookup.
4. Write takeaway titles for every slide (conclusion, not description). Squint test: can a stranger get the story from titles alone?
5. Build an appendix: methodology, data sources, the queries behind the charts. Then rehearse a 5-minute delivery and time it.
handsOnLab.title: Executive storytelling deck lab

choices: Restructure to answer-first: one takeaway title per slide stating the recommendation and its evidence, move the 30 exploration slides to the appendix, rehearse the 5-minute version
Make the fonts bigger and hope
Send the 40 slides by email instead
mockTask.explain: The failure is structural: exploration ≠ story. Executives need the recommendation with its evidence up front; the 30 slides become an appendix for the one person who asks.
mockTask.q: You have 10 minutes with the CFO. Your draft has 40 slides of thorough exploration. The feedback from your dry run: 'I don't know what you're asking me to decide.' Your fix:
